items.title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And you know we were friends from early days right up until she passed away.

ctx.x: One of my favorite tracks on this Billy Taylor with Four Flutes record was a composition that I have never heard from Mary Lou Williams Cubano. Has she ever recorded that or…

I don’t know if she recorded it but she used to play… Mary Lou and I worked opposite of one another on many occasions, at Downbeat, at the Composer and at several… at Café Society and even earlier then that. So every opportunity I got to be around her or to work opposite of her was a welcomed opportunity. And you know we were friends from early days right up until she passed away. So I knew that tune. I had heard her do that a lot. And actually it is nothing but a base line. There is no melody. It is just a bass…
When you were recording with Riverside I think this is a significant point; the whole concept of stereo came into being. What was that like? How did it change recording?

items.title: 53571_Mary Lou Williams oral history interview
items.q: when I got this job I was alternating with Billy Taylor.

ctx.x: I don't know what happened because see I was working on the East Side and various places out of the city, but when I got this job I was alternating with Billy Taylor. I can't remember the name of this place, at 52nd and Eighth Avenue. So I had a way of always helping musicians. At one time I was recording for Moe Asch and what happened, he was expecting a pianist and I had taken Bill Coleman and Al Hail with me and he got a little peeved about it but he recorded it, because they were out of work and I put them…
